# 1 Samuel 5 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

This chapter narrates what happened when the Philistines placed the captured Ark of the Covenant in their own territory. The Ark travels through three Philistine cities—Ashdod, Gath, and Ekron—and in each place the LORD demonstrates His supremacy over Dagon and afflicts the people with judgment. The major theological point is that God will glorify Himself even among His enemies; His presence brings either blessing or curse depending on the heart's response (cf. 2 Cor 2:15–16). Several commentators note the parallels between this chapter and the plagues on Egypt (Exodus 7–12) as demonstrations of Yahweh's sovereignty.

**Sources:** Enduring Word; Constable; Gill; Ellicott via StudyLight; Pulpit Commentary via StudyLight; Precept Austin

---

## v. 1 — "After the Philistines had captured the ark of God, they took it from Ebenezer to Ashdod"

- **The journey from Ebenezer to Ashdod.** Ashdod was one of the five principal Philistine cities, about 20–30 miles southwest of Ebenezer and about 3 miles from the Mediterranean coast. It was one of the most prominent Philistine cities and contained a famous temple of Dagon. *(Gill: biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/5.htm; Constable: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-5.html)*

- **"The ark of God."** The narrator pointedly calls it the *ark of God*, not merely a captured trophy. Though Israel had treated it superstitiously (ch. 4), it remained God's holy possession. *(Enduring Word: enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-5/)*

- **Which Ebenezer?** This Ebenezer (the battle site of ch. 4) is likely not the same location as the memorial stone Samuel later set up between Mizpah and Shen (1 Sam 7:12). *(Precept Austin: preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-5-commentary)*

- **Why Ashdod?** It may have been the nearest major Philistine city following the battle. Gill suggests it was perhaps the most famous of their cities. *(Gill: biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/5.htm)*

---

## v. 2 — "carried it into the temple of Dagon, and set it beside his statue"

- **A trophy in Dagon's temple.** Placing the captured Ark beside the image of Dagon was a symbolic act declaring Dagon's superiority over Yahweh. The Philistines believed their god had defeated Israel's God in battle. It was the ancient Near Eastern custom to place captured religious objects in the temple of the conquering deity. *(Enduring Word: enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-5/; Constable: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-5.html)*

- **Who was Dagon?** Dagon was the chief deity of the Philistines, likely a grain/fertility god (cf. Heb. *dagan* = grain) whose worship began in Mesopotamia around 2500 B.C. The popular conception pictures him as half-man, half-fish (from Heb. *dag* = fish). He was thought to be the father of Baal. *(Constable; Precept Austin; Enduring Word: citing Keil & Delitzsch)*

- Gill notes that some Jewish interpreters (Abarbinel) thought the Philistines placed the Ark beside Dagon *in honour to the ark*, as pagans would sometimes add foreign gods to their own pantheon. Others, like Procopius Gazaeus, understood it as a trophy of victory. *(Gill: biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/5.htm)*

- **Precept Austin** draws a parallel with Judges 16:23–30, where the Philistines earlier credited Dagon with delivering Samson into their hands — only for Samson to destroy Dagon's temple. Both episodes show the Philistines wrongly assuming Dagon had triumphed over Yahweh. *(Precept Austin: preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-5-commentary)*

---

## v. 3 — "When the people of Ashdod got up early the next morning, there was Dagon, fallen on his face before the ark of the LORD. So they took Dagon and returned him to his place."

- **Dagon prostrate in worship.** The posture of falling on one's face was a posture of worship and homage. The irony is unmistakable: the idol that supposedly had defeated Yahweh is now bowing before the symbol of His presence. God will glorify Himself, even when men will not. *(Enduring Word: enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-5/; Constable: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-5.html)*

- **They set him back up.** The Philistines attributed the fall to chance — an accident. Gill notes they "had no notion that it was owing to the ark of God, or to the God of Israel." They simply repositioned the idol and thought nothing more of it. *(Gill: biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/5.htm)*

- **Ellicott** observes that the Philistines had grown up with awe of the "golden chest." They were reluctant to see anything supernatural in the event. *(Ellicott: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-5.html)*

- **The first warning ignored.** This is the pattern: God gave a relatively gentle sign (the idol merely fallen), but the Philistines ignored it and restored their idol. When we close our ears to God's first, quieter word, He often speaks again in ways we will not like. *(Enduring Word: enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-5/)*

---

## v. 4 — "But when they got up early the next morning, there was Dagon, fallen on his face before the ark of the LORD, with his head and his hands broken off and lying on the threshold. Only the torso remained."

- **A second, more devastating fall.** This time Dagon not only fell but was mutilated. The head (symbolizing wisdom and sovereign control) and the hands/palms (symbolizing power and strength) were severed. This signified that Dagon had neither wisdom nor power — he was utterly impotent before the LORD. *(Gill: biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/5.htm; Constable: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-5.html)*

- **Head and hands on the threshold.** Constable notes that in ancient Near Eastern warfare, victors cut off the heads and hands of slain enemies to count the dead (cf. 1 Sam 29:4; Judg 8:6). The imagery is that Yahweh has defeated Dagon in battle. The threshold itself became the instrument of Dagon's decapitation, making it sacred (or accursed) in Philistine eyes. *(Constable: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-5.html)*

- **"Only Dagon was left" — the fish part.** Gill, citing the medieval Jewish commentator Kimchi, explains that Dagon was imagined as a man from the navel upward and a fish from the navel downward. The Hebrew text literally says "only Dagon was left," which Gill interprets as the fishy (lower) part remaining — a further humiliation. *(Gill: biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/5.htm)*

- **An emblem of idolatry's fall.** Gill also sees this as a typological picture: the fall of idolatry in the Gentile world before the preaching of the Gospel, and the fall of "the idol of man's righteousness" before the righteousness of Christ. *(Gill: biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/5.htm)*

- **Constable notes** that later Goliath (the Philistine champion) would also fall on his face before David (1 Sam 17:49), and the Philistines would cut off Saul's head (1 Chr 10:10) — ironic echoes of this passage. *(Constable: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-5.html)*

---

## v. 5 — "That is why, to this day, the priests of Dagon and all who enter the temple of Dagon in Ashdod do not step on the threshold."

- **Origin of a superstitious custom.** Rather than abandon Dagon and turn to the LORD, the Philistine priests created a religious tradition: they would not tread on the threshold. Enduring Word emphasizes that this was a tragic choice — they had clear evidence of God's supremacy but chose "a religious tradition instead" rather than repentance. *(Enduring Word: enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-5/)*

- **"To this day."** This phrase indicates the custom persisted until the time of the writing of 1 Samuel (and apparently beyond). Zephaniah 1:9, written in the reign of Josiah, condemns "all those who leap on [or over] the threshold," likely alluding to this very Philistine practice. *(Ellicott: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-5.html; Gill: biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/5.htm)*

- **Sacred threshold.** In the ancient world, sanctuary thresholds commonly marked the boundary between sacred and profane space. This incident rendered Dagon's threshold even more superstitiously sacred. *(Constable: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-5.html)*

- **Differing views on the meaning of leaping over:** Some commentators think the threshold was considered holy because Dagon touched it; others think it was treated with detestation because it had been the means of decapitating their god. Gill inclines toward the latter view. *(Gill: biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/5.htm)*

---

## v. 6 — "Now the hand of the LORD was heavy on the people of Ashdod and its vicinity, ravaging them and afflicting them with tumors."

- **"The hand of the LORD."** This anthropomorphic phrase is the major theme of the ark narrative, occurring nine times in 1 Samuel 4–7. It represents Yahweh in active judgment. In the biblical world, sickness and death were understood as the effects of a deity's "hand." *(Constable: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-5.html)*

- **From the idol to the people.** God first struck their god; now He strikes them. Having ignored the first (gentler) warning of Dagon's fall, the Philistines now face a heavier word: physical affliction. *(Enduring Word: enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-5/)*

- **What were the "tumors"?** This is debated among commentators:

  - **Traditional view: hemorrhoids.** Older commentators (Gill, Keil & Delitzsch, Clarke) describe them as bleeding piles or haemorrhoids. The Hebrew word *'ophalim* (from *'aphal*, "to be elevated, to swell") means swellings or tumours. The synagogue never read this word aloud; the reader substituted *tehorim*, indicating the word was considered indecent. Gill notes Josephus thought it was dysentery or "bloody flux," and Kimchi called it "a very painful disease, from whence comes a great quantity of blood." *(Gill: biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/5.htm; Pulpit Commentary via studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-5.html)*

  - **Modern view: bubonic plague.** More recent commentators (Youngblood, Constable, Enduring Word) argue for bubonic plague because: (1) the disease was epidemic and associated with panic and high death rates; (2) the Philistines associated it with mice/rats (1 Sam 6:4–5), which carry bubonic plague; (3) the Septuagint adds that "mice were produced in the land"; (4) the tumors (buboes) appeared in the groin area, which is characteristic of bubonic plague. *(Enduring Word: enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-5/; Constable: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-5.html)*

  - **Pulpit Commentary** notes the Septuagint addition about mice may be a later gloss to explain the golden mice of 1 Sam 6:4–5, not original to the Hebrew text. The mouse was an ancient symbol of pestilence (Herodotus 2:141). *(Pulpit Commentary via studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-5.html)*

---

## v. 7 — "And when the men of Ashdod saw what was happening, they said, 'The ark of the God of Israel must not stay here with us, because His hand is heavy upon us and upon our god Dagon.'"

- **They correctly identify the cause.** The men of Ashdod rightly attributed their affliction to "the God of Israel" — not to chance or natural causes. They acknowledged "His hand is heavy upon us and upon Dagon our god." This is a remarkable confession from pagans. *(Gill: biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/5.htm; Constable: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-5.html)*

- **But they still do not repent.** They recognize Yahweh's power but choose to send Him away rather than submit to Him. Gill compares them to the Gergesenes who begged Jesus to leave their region (Matt 8:34), "having more regard for their swine than for him." *(Gill: biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/5.htm)*

- **Constable** observes: "The people of Ashdod should have turned from worshipping Dagon and put their trust in Yahweh. Death followed because they chose to continue in unbelief in spite of their confession of Yahweh's superiority." *(Constable: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-5.html)*

---

## v. 8 — "So they called together all the rulers of the Philistines and asked, 'What shall we do with the ark of the God of Israel?' 'It must be moved to Gath,' they replied. So they carried away the ark of the God of Israel."

- **The five lords convened.** The Philistines had a confederacy of five city-states (Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron — Josh 13:3), each ruled by a "lord." The men of Ashdod could not unilaterally dispose of the Ark; they needed the consent of all five lords. *(Gill: biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/5.htm)*

- **"Let it be carried to Gath."** Some versions (Septuagint, Vulgate) render this as the men of Gath themselves volunteering: "Let the ark of God come to us." Gill suggests the Gathites may have suspected the disease was merely a local pestilence, not a divine judgment, and thus were willing to receive the Ark. *(Gill: biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/5.htm)*

- **"Carried about."** Gill notes the Hebrew suggests they carried it in a roundabout way, "as if they had a mind to give it an airing, before they fixed it any where" — another attempt to deny supernatural causation. *(Gill: biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/5.htm)*

- **Gath** (lit. "winepress") lay about 12 miles southeast of Ashdod. *(Constable: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-5.html)*

---

## v. 9 — "But after they had moved the ark to Gath, the LORD's hand was also against that city, throwing it into great confusion and afflicting the men of the city, both young and old, with an outbreak of tumors."

- **The judgment follows the Ark.** Moving the Ark to a new location did not solve the problem, because the problem was not the location but unrepentant hearts. "The city of Gath didn't do any better than the city of Ashdod." *(Enduring Word: enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-5/)*

- **"A very great destruction."** Gill notes the judgment at Gath was "greater than that at Ashdod, more persons were destroyed; the distemper sent among them was more epidemic and mortal." The phrase "both small and great" indicates every social class was afflicted. *(Gill: biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/5.htm)*

- **The Hebrew word translated "broke out"** occurs only here in the Old Testament. The Septuagint interpreted it as referring to the groin area, which supports the bubonic plague identification (buboes in the groin are characteristic). *(Constable: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-5.html)*

- **Gill adds a wrinkle on the nature of the tumors at Gath:** "the emerods were hidden unto them" — they were more inward, internal, and therefore "more painful, and not so easy to come at, and more difficult of cure" than those at Ashdod. *(Gill: biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/5.htm)*

---

## v. 10 — "So they sent the ark of God to Ekron, but as it arrived, the Ekronites cried out, 'They have brought us the ark of the God of Israel in order to kill us and our people!'"

- **Ekron: the third city.** Ekron was another of the five Philistine principalities, about 6 miles north of Gath. It was the city where Baal-Zebub (the "lord of the fly") was worshipped. *(Gill: biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/5.htm; Constable: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-5.html)*

- **The reputation preceded the Ark.** By now, word had spread about what happened in Ashdod and Gath. The Ekronites immediately recognized the Ark not as a trophy but as "a divine instrument of death." They protested before the Ark even arrived. *(Constable: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-5.html)*

- **"To kill us and our people."** This is not hyperbole — people were actually dying. The Ekronites understood that receiving the Ark was a death sentence. *(Enduring Word: enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-5/)*

---

## v. 11 — "Then the Ekronites assembled all the rulers of the Philistines and said, 'Send away the ark of the God of Israel. It must return to its place, so that it will not kill us and our people!' For a deadly confusion had pervaded the city; the hand of God was heavy upon it."

- **The second council of lords.** This is the second time all five Philistine lords are summoned (first in v. 8). The Ekronites demanded a united decision to send the Ark back. *(Gill: biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/5.htm)*

- **"A deadly confusion."** The Pulpit Commentary notes that the Hebrew word here suggests not just disease but panic and terror — a "deadly destruction" (as in the KJV) that included both the plague and the psychological horror of knowing God's hand was against them. *(Pulpit Commentary via studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-5.html)*

- **"The hand of God was very heavy there."** Gill observes the suffering at Ekron seems even worse than at Ashdod and Gath, "which made them the more pressing to get rid of the ark." The judgment escalated at each stop. *(Gill: biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/5.htm)*

- **"Let it go back to its own place."** The Philistine lords acknowledged the Ark belonged in Israel — specifically, they likely had Shiloh in mind, though the Ark never returned there. *(Gill: biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/5.htm)*

- **Ellicott** reflects on the pathos of the Philistines' situation: they had long desired to capture this "golden chest" that had once led Israel to victory under Joshua. Now they possessed it — and it was destroying them. They were deeply reluctant to surrender their trophy, which is why they tried city after city before finally conceding. *(Ellicott: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-5.html)*

---

## v. 12 — "Those who did not die were afflicted with tumors, and the outcry of the city went up to heaven."

- **Death and disease together.** The verse distinguishes between those who died (apparently from the pestilence or "deadly destruction") and those who survived but were afflicted with the tumors. This confirms that the tumors alone were not the cause of death — there was a separate, mortal element to the judgment. *(Gill: biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/5.htm)*

- **"The cry of the city went up to heaven."** This is not a cry of repentance or prayer to Yahweh; it is a cry of anguish and distress. The Pulpit Commentary distinguishes this word from v. 10's "outcry of indignation" — here it is "a cry for help, a cry of sorrow." The phrase echoes the great cry in Egypt at the death of the firstborn (Exod 12:30). *(Pulpit Commentary via studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-5.html; Constable: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-5.html)*

- **Seven months of judgment.** The next chapter (1 Sam 6:1) notes the Ark remained in Philistine territory for seven months. Throughout this period, the Philistines learned what Israel had not yet grasped: Yahweh is the sovereign God. Yet — tragically — "they refused to bow before Him and so experienced death, though the Lord mixed mercy with judgment and did not kill all the Philistines." *(Constable: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-5.html)*

- **A historical memory.** Gill notes that Herodotus records a tradition that the Scythians, having plundered the temple of Venus at Ashkelon (another Philistine city), were afflicted with "the female disease" (haemorrhoids) — indicating the memory of what the Philistines suffered for their sacrilege endured for centuries. *(Gill: biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/5.htm)*

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

Based on the sources accessed, here are distinct emphases:

### Charismatic / Pentecostal (Enduring Word — David Guzik)
- Strong emphasis on the *experiential* dimension: God "will glorify Himself" and we must not harden our hearts when He speaks through circumstances. The "presence of God" functions like a fragrance of life or death depending on the heart. Practical application is central. *(enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-5/)*

### Older Baptist / Reformed Baptist (Gill, 18th century)
- Typological reading: Dagon's fall as an emblem of the fall of idolatry before the Gospel, and of "the idol of man's righteousness" falling before the righteousness of Christ. More doctrinal and typological emphasis than modern commentaries. *(Gill: biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/5.htm)*

### Reformed Baptist (John Piper / Desiring God)
- Not a verse-by-verse commentary, but Piper uses 1 Samuel 5–6 to discuss the nature of idolatry: idols are "anything that we come to rely on for some blessing, or help, or guidance in the place of a wholehearted reliance on the true and living God." He notes the golden tumors and mice were "trinkets" to ward off evil — idolatrous talismans. *(desiringgod.org/interviews/what-is-an-idol)*

### Evangelical / Dispensational (Constable, DTS)
- Emphasis on the historical-contextual: the ancient Near Eastern practice of cutting off heads and hands of enemies, the geography of Philistine cities, archaeological data, and the Septuagint's interpretive additions. Focus on "the hand of the Lord" as a structuring theological motif (9 occurrences). *(studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-5.html)*

### Anglican (Ellicott, 19th century)
- Ellicott's tone is more reflective and homiletic: he draws out the pathos of the Philistine lords torn between pride in their trophy and the devastation it brings. He asks, "Is there not an unseen power ever protecting God's institutions, His ordinances, and His ritual… even though all these things, owing to the faults and errors of His servants, have lost apparently their holy and beneficial influence?" — a distinctly Anglican concern for the sanctity of sacred things. *(studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-5.html)*

### Modern Scholarship
- **The Ark Narrative hypothesis** (referenced by Constable): Critical scholars have argued that 1 Sam 4:1b–7:1 and 2 Samuel 6 are fragments of an older, independent "Ark Narrative" source document. Of 61 references to the ark in 1–2 Samuel, 36 appear in 4:1b–7:2. Conservative scholars generally dispute this, seeing the emphasis as thematic rather than evidence of a separate source. *(Constable: studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-5.html)*
